headline: Stellwagen Basin holding haddock on the mud, gravel edges still giving up cod at 110 feet
subhead: Bluefin are still working the mackerel schools on top of the Bank, but the fleet's split on where the best grade of groundfish is sitting this week.
body_markdown:
Sixty-eight degrees on the surface over the Basin, dropping into the low 50s once you punch through the thermocline around 90 feet — that's the number that matters right now on Stellwagen. The top of the water column is still carrying summer heat, but underneath it the Bank is behaving like it should for early September: cod tucked into the gravel on the edges, haddock spread out on the mud in the deeper basin, and bluefin still working the surface wherever the mackerel bunch up tight enough to get pinned.

The warm signature that's carried this whole summer hasn't cracked yet. We flagged it last week — said if that warm water held, the pattern would hold with it — and it has. Boats running deep-drop gear for swordfish have been finding fish farther north into Gulf of Maine water than is typical for this time of year, working the drop-offs toward Carter Canyon in 500-plus feet. That's not a groundfish signal, but it's confirmation the warm regime is still sitting on top of us. It won't last forever. Once that layer breaks down — and it will, probably with the first real cool front of the month — expect the whole Bank to reset toward a more typical fall pattern fast.

Until then, the groundfish bite is steady but not blow-the-doors-off. Cod are coming off the gravel patches on Stellwagen Edge, mostly in 100 to 130 feet, with the better fish running 8 to 15 pounds mixed with a lot of shorts that need to go back. Jigging diamond jigs tipped with a squid strip is still outfishing bait on the drift — a 12-ounce diamond with a single mackerel-belly strip, worked with a short hop off bottom, has been the go-to for boats staying disciplined about keeping the jig ticking the gravel instead of ripping it too high. Bait soakers doing clam or herring on a high-low rig are getting fish too, but they're working harder for it — the cod have been more willing to chase a moving bait than sit and wait on this warm water.

Haddock are the more consistent story. The mud bottom in Stellwagen Basin, running 180 to 220 feet, has been giving up a steady grade of haddock in the 2 to 5 pound class, with the occasional 8-pounder mixed in to keep things interesting. Standard haddock rigs — a two-hook high-low with clam bellies or squid, fished right on bottom with just enough weight to hold in the current — are doing the work. The bite window has been tide-dependent more than time-of-day dependent: the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood have been producing the tightest bunches of bites, which tracks with how haddock stack up on structure when the current is moving enough to keep bait suspended but not so hard it's pinning gear sideways.

Pollock have been scattered along the steeper drop-offs near Tillies Bank, mostly suspended 40 to 60 feet down over deeper water, and they've been a bonus fish more than a target — a few boats jigging bucktails or heavy diamond jigs for cod have picked off pollock to 10 pounds on the same drops. Hake reports have been thinner this week; a few boats working the deeper current lines off the Basin at night have scratched out a few, but it hasn't been consistent enough to call it a pattern yet.

The bluefin story is the one everybody at the dock wants to talk about, and it's mixed. When the mackerel schools bunch up tight on top of the Bank — usually mid-morning once the sun's had a chance to push bait up — the tuna show and the bite can turn into a genuine spectacle for twenty or thirty minutes before it shuts back off. Chunking with fresh mackerel over a slick has worked when boats can find and hold on a school, and a few jig-and-pop guys throwing stickbaits into visible surface activity have connected on smaller fish in the 60 to 100 pound class. But it's not a bite you can plan a whole trip around yet — more than one boat has spent hours running the Bank without finding fish committed enough to feed. Patience and mobility matter more than gear right now.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern holds if the warm water holds — light winds and a building moon into the weekend should keep the Bank fishable and the tide cycles workable for both the gravel bite and the mud bite. If there's a shift worth watching, it's the same one we flagged before: any real cool front pushing through New England in the next week to two weeks is going to start knocking that surface layer down, and when it does, expect the cod to push shallower onto the edges as the water column evens out, and expect the tuna bite to either sharpen up on a final feed before the mackerel scatter, or shut down hard if the bait pushes out ahead of the cold. For now, if there's only one day to spend on the Bank, split it — work the gravel on Stellwagen Edge early on the last of the ebb for cod, then swing to the Basin mud for haddock once the tide turns, and keep an eye on the horizon for birds working bait in case the bluefin decide to show.
